title: Impact of Political Turnover on Public Spending

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Causal method: Instrumental‐Variables (2SLS).  
Rationale: Democratic control (x) may be endogenous to unobserved local characteristics that also affect spending (y). A “close-election Democratic win” (z) provides quasi-random variation in party control that is plausibly unrelated to those unobservables, supplying an instrument.  

Key assumptions  
• Relevance: z is strongly correlated with Democratic control (Cov(z,x) ≠ 0).  
• Exogeneity / exclusion: Conditional on controls, z affects public spending only through its effect on Democratic control (Cov(z,ε) = 0).  
• Monotonicity (for LATE interpretation): a close win cannot make a jurisdiction less likely to be Democratic.  

## 2. R Code
```r
# ---------- 0. Packages ----------
required <- c("readr", "AER", "sandwich", "lmtest")
new      <- required[!(required %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"])]
if(length(new)) install.packages(new, repos = "https://cran.r-project.org")
lapply(required, library, character.only = TRUE)

# ---------- 1. Load data ----------
dat_path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s74_data.csv"
df <- read_csv(dat_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

# ---------- 2. Naïve OLS ----------
ols <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = df)
ols_robust_se <- coeftest(ols, vcov = vcovHC(ols, type = "HC1"))

cat("\nNaïve OLS (robust SE):\n")
print(ols_robust_se["x",])

# ---------- 3. First stage ----------
fs <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = df)
fs_robust <- coeftest(fs, vcov = vcovHC(fs, type = "HC1"))
F_stat <- waldtest(fs, "z", vcov = vcovHC(fs, type = "HC1"))$F[2]

cat("\nFirst-stage coefficient on z (robust SE):\n")
print(fs_robust["z",])
cat(sprintf("First-stage F-statistic on instrument z: %.2f\n", F_stat))

# ---------- 4. 2SLS ----------
iv <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df)
iv_robust_se <- coeftest(iv, vcov = vcovHC(iv, type = "HC1"))

cat("\n2SLS estimate (robust SE):\n")
print(iv_robust_se["x",])

# ---------- 5. Reduced form ----------
rf <- lm(y ~ z + controls, data = df)
rf_robust <- coeftest(rf, vcov = vcovHC(rf, type = "HC1"))

cat("\nReduced-form effect of z on y (robust SE):\n")
print(rf_robust["z",])

# ---------- 6. Anderson–Rubin test (weak-IV robust inference) ----------
ar_test <- linearHypothesis(iv, "x = 0", test = "Chisq", vcov = vcovHC(iv, type = "HC1"))
cat("\nAnderson-Rubin test of H0: effect = 0\n")
print(ar_test)

# ---------- 7. Summary output ----------
cat("\n--- Summary ---\n")
cat(sprintf("Naïve OLS coefficient on x:  %.4f (robust SE %.4f)\n",
            ols_robust_se["x","Estimate"], ols_robust_se["x","Std. Error"]))
cat(sprintf("2SLS coefficient on x:       %.4f (robust SE %.4f)\n",
            iv_robust_se["x","Estimate"], iv_robust_se["x","Std. Error"]))
cat(sprintf("First-stage F-statistic:     %.2f\n", F_stat))
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Sign: Positive. A Democratic victory is anticipated to raise log public spending.  
Magnitude: In logs, a 0/1 change from Republican to Democratic control may increase spending by roughly 0.25–0.40 log-points (≈ 28–50 %). OLS may show a smaller effect (≈ 0.15) due to downward bias from strategic fiscal conservatism in competitive districts, whereas the 2SLS estimate should lie nearer the upper half of that range if the instrument is strong.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use close-election Democratic wins as an instrument for Democratic control.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The analysis suggests a negative causal impact of Democratic control on public spending.
